title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) basics
notes: RAG means retrieve the relevant chunks, add them to the prompt, and generate the answer from them.
Keyword scoring is a simple start; embeddings in a vector store such as Chroma or pgvector match meaning, not just words.
Answer only from retrieved text, say so when it doesn't cover the question, and keep your sources current.

slides.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) basics
slides.sub: Answer from Orbit's own documents instead of the model's best guess
sentences: Remember the early Scout that promised a ninety day refund Orbit never offered?
The model filled a gap with something that sounded right.
In this lesson you will learn RAG, the standard way to make an agent answer from your own documents.

slides.title: Why not paste every document in?

left.label: Paste every document
points: Slow and costly as documents grow

right.label: Retrieve what's relevant
points: The model sees the right text

sentences: Why not simply paste every document into the system prompt?
For one short file, like Orbit's six-section policy, that honestly works.
But Orbit's documents keep growing: size guides, care instructions, shipping rules, and more.
Pasting all of it into every call is slow and costly, and the one line that matters gets buried.
The better way is to find the few passages that answer this question, and send only those.
That approach scales from six sections to six thousand pages.

slides.title: So what is RAG?
slides.definition: Retrieval-augmented generation: find the passages that answer a question, add them to the prompt, and let the model answer from them.

parts.text: Augment: add it to the prompt

analogy.label: Think of it as
analogy.text: An open-book exam. The student still writes the answer, but from the right page of the book, not from memory.

sentences: This pattern has a name: RAG, short for retrieval-augmented generation.
Retrieve means finding the passages in your documents that relate to the question.
Augment means adding those passages to the prompt, right next to the question.
Generate means the model writes its answer from that text.
It's an open-book exam. The student still writes the answer, but from the right page, not from memory.

slides.title: RAG, step by step

note.text: Split once, ahead of time. Search and answer on every question.

sentences: Let's walk through it with Orbit's policy file.
You start with your documents.
Ahead of time, you split them into chunks, small passages that make sense on their own, like one section of the policy.
When a question arrives, you score every chunk against it and keep the best two or three.
Those chunks go into the prompt, together with the question.
The model answers from them, or says plainly that they don't cover the question.
Splitting happens once. Searching and answering happen for every question.

slides.title: Owen's question, answered from two chunks

messages.label: Owen
messages.text: My new jacket is too big. Can I send it back, and is return shipping free? It was $310.

messages.label: search_policy
messages.text: Top 2 of 6 sections: Return shipping (3 shared words), Returns (2)

messages.label: Added to the prompt
messages.text: Return shipping is free on orders over $75... You can return any unused item within 30 days of delivery...

messages.label: Scout
messages.text: Yes! Unused items can come back within 30 days of delivery, in the original packaging. Your order was over $75, so return shipping is free.

aside.label: Grounded
aside.text: Every claim in the reply traces back to a line of Orbit's policy.

sentences: Here's RAG in a real Orbit chat.
Owen's new jacket is too big, and he wants to know if he can send it back for free.
Scout searches the policy, and the two best-matching sections come back: return shipping, and returns.
Those two chunks are added to the prompt.
Scout answers from them: unused items within thirty days, and free return shipping on orders over seventy-five dollars.
Every claim in that answer traces back to a line of Orbit's policy.

slides.title: Two ways to find the best chunks

left.label: Keyword scoring
points: Count words shared with the question
A few lines of Python, no extra service
Misses synonyms: send back versus return

right.label: Embeddings
points: Text turned into numbers that capture meaning
Finds similar meaning in different words
Kept in a vector store: Chroma, pgvector

sentences: How do you score the chunks? There are two common ways.
The simple way is keyword scoring: count the words each chunk shares with the question.
It needs no extra service and fits in a few lines of Python. It's what you will build today.
Its weakness is synonyms. Send it back and return mean the same thing, but share no words.
The real-project way is embeddings: a model turns each chunk into a list of numbers that captures its meaning.
Chunks with similar meaning get similar numbers, so a question finds them even in different words.
Those numbers live in a vector store, such as Chroma or pgvector, which searches millions of chunks quickly.

slides.title: Rules that make RAG trustworthy
slides.lead: Retrieval finds the text. The prompt decides how the model uses it.

bullets.text: Answer only from the retrieved text
Not covered? Say so, and offer a person
Keep sources current: remove old versions, date every file
Show which section the answer came from

aside.label: Garbage in, garbage out
aside.text: Retrieval can't fix a wrong document. If last year's policy is in the folder, it can be retrieved.

sentences: Finding the right text is half the job. The prompt does the other half.
Tell the model to answer only from the retrieved text, not from what shops usually do.
If the chunks don't cover the question, it should say so plainly and offer to pass it to a person.
Keep your sources clean: remove old versions, and put a date on every file.
And show which section an answer came from, so Leo's team can check it in seconds.
Retrieval can't fix a wrong document. If last year's policy is still in the folder, it can be retrieved.

slides.title: search_policy in a few lines
slides.lead: Split policy.md at its headings, score each section by shared words, return the best two.

rows.code: best = [s for s in scored[:top] if s[0] > 0]

aside.label: In real projects
aside.text: Swap the scoring for embeddings and a vector store. The tool's name and inputs stay the same.

sentences: Here's the heart of the search tool you will write in the guided practice.
It splits the policy file at each heading, so every section becomes a chunk.
For each chunk, it counts the words shared with the query.
It sorts the chunks, highest score first.
And it returns the top two, skipping any chunk that shares no words at all.
Later you can swap the scoring for embeddings, and Scout won't notice the difference.

slides.title: What to take away

points.text: RAG: retrieve relevant text, add it to the prompt, answer from it.
Split documents into chunks once; search them on every question.
Keyword scoring is simple; embeddings and a vector store catch meaning.
Answer only from the chunks, and say so when they don't cover it.

sentences: Let's recap.
RAG means retrieve the relevant text, add it to the prompt, and generate the answer from it.
You split documents into chunks once, and search them for every question.
Keyword scoring is a fine start. Embeddings in a vector store catch meaning in real projects.
The model answers only from what was retrieved, and says so when that doesn't cover the question.
Next: what Scout should do when one request needs several steps.

midQuiz.q: In RAG, what goes into the prompt along with the customer's question?
options: The few chunks that best match the question
A list of the customer's past chats
midQuiz.explain: Retrieval picks the best-matching chunks, and only those are added. That keeps the request small and focused.
midQuiz.hint: The R in RAG stands for retrieve. What gets retrieved?

midQuiz.q: A customer asks about gift wrapping. The retrieved chunks are about shipping times. What should Scout do?
options: Answer from what shops usually do
Say the policy doesn't cover it and offer a person
Adapt the closest chunk into an answer
midQuiz.explain: The model should answer only from retrieved text. When that text doesn't cover the question, saying so is the honest answer.
midQuiz.hint: Does any retrieved line actually mention gift wrapping?

endQuiz.q: A customer asks if she can send her boots back. Keyword scoring misses the Returns section. What would catch it?
options: Embeddings, which match meaning rather than exact words
Returning only the single best chunk
endQuiz.explain: Send back and return share no words, so keyword scoring misses the match. Embeddings place similar meanings close together.
endQuiz.hint: The problem is two different words for the same idea.

endQuiz.q: Why split documents into chunks instead of retrieving whole files?
options: Chunks let you send only the passages that matter
The API only accepts text in chunks
endQuiz.explain: Small chunks keep requests short and put the right lines in front of the model, instead of burying them in a long file.
endQuiz.hint: Think back to why pasting every document was a problem.
